item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
So, it's a contract that adds terms to itself, which the signatory is compelled to fulfill. This contrasts with the sort of tone that's set by making it a contract in the first place — you can't consider all the terms of the agreement before signing on.

That could be fine — we have plenty of things that screw your over unfairly — except it doesn't do so in an interesting way. You just comply 'til you die. Comply with what? [DATA EXPUNGED].

This needs a good "why" and "how" before it can really make the most of its current potential.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
However, the complexity of the terms and demands increases with the number of amendments fulfilled, eventually reaching extremes including but not limited to: the murder of staff members, the removal of SCP-350 from Foundation containment, and even [DATA EXPUNGED]

Here's an idea: 350 seems to have an agenda of it's own. It wants/needs to be signed, and have its conditions acted upon. As currently written, this agenda is only barely hinted at.

Perhaps if we had some (any) information on its prior behavior, such as the last individual to possess the document prior to its containment by the Foundation and what conditions that individual had tried/was trying to fulfill, this SCP could move up in the rankings.

As it stands, it's really pretty light on plot. Did it simply show up at Site…uh…where is it again? How was it discovered? Is there a watermark or letterhead that may shed some light on its origins or purpose?

-1 until apparent seed grows into an SCP.

item.title: Re: Confused
item.content:encoded:
Safe does not mean harmless. It means "it will not actively try to escape, and will not kill you as long as you follow the Special Containment Procedures" An atom bomb would be safe. They do nothing as long as you don't install the firing mechanism, enter the activation code into the mechanical safety release correctly on the first try (or the internal mechanisms will tear themselves apart and render the entire device inoperative), and slam them into something really hard.

For contrast, keter does not mean "really deadly", it means "This is really hard to contain, and its very existence is potentially harmful to normalcy." Something completely harmless with noble intentions can be keter: see SCP-2137.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Very much, I agree with this. The damn thing cheats.

Sign a contract, wire money, get a deep desire fulfilled - check. I'm good with all that, it's a great SCP.

…suddenly, having to complete extra services/provide more in return for the item already received?

BZZZZT. Instant lack of interest. With sufficient data/the whole story, no one would ever sign the thing. …so I can see it wanting out from under the Foundation's thumb, so it can find people who don't know it freaking cheats on the contract.

…what happens if I tear off the 49 blank pages, shred them, and sign on the bottom of page 1? :D

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Must be the lawyer in me, but I don't like the internal inconsistency. i.e. the document purports to follow laws, but the addition of new terms to a concluded contract can never be lawfully enforced or contractually effective, unless there is agreement between the parties on a variety of matters (e.g. the terms, the price, etc).

It might work better if the subsequent terms offered something even more desirable, in return for a more horrible price. The contract would be become effective either by signature or by mental consent.

Things that the Foundation is containing do not need to be things that need a constant stream of bodies thrown on top of them to keep them busy or sated. We've got lots of things that are listed as safe and can be locked in a drawer that are still creepy or interesting. If the contract can really give you your wildest dreams, your containment procedures could certainly focus on keeping people AWAY from it rather than vice versa, no need to throw on some forced sense of danger to keep the contract from getting out.

Also: It doesn't need to be part of the article but I am super curious about that bank account.
